planting.note: Scatter seed onto bare, thin dolomite or limestone soil in autumn so it can germinate with fall rains and overwinter as a low rosette, since this winter annual blooms the following spring and dies after setting seed.

directions: Grow in shallow, rocky, alkaline soil over exposed dolomite, the specific glade habitat this federally studied winter annual naturally occupies in a handful of southwestern Missouri counties. A basal rosette of gray-green leaves sends up short flowering stalks topped with small four-petaled yellow flowers in late winter and early spring, followed by distinctive inflated, bladder-like seed pods that give the plant its common name. Populations were once federally listed as threatened before recovering enough for delisting in 2003, and the species still depends on open, lightly disturbed glade rock free of heavy leaf litter or encroaching woody growth. It completes its entire life cycle before the heat of summer and self-sows reliably where competition stays low.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Direct sow onto thin, open glade soil near established native warm-season bunchgrasses such as little bluestem, since this facultative hemiparasite taps the roots of nearby grasses for part of its nutrition and performs poorly in isolation.

directions: Plant in thin, rocky, well-drained soil over exposed limestone or dolomite in full sun, the open glade and barrens habitat this annual shares with native bunchgrasses across the Interior Highlands and limestone cedar glade regions. Wiry stems carry narrow leaves and small tubular pink flowers with a darker throat that open for a single day in late summer and early fall, drawing bumblebees as primary pollinators. As a hemiparasite it forms root connections to nearby grasses, so gardeners should site it alongside little bluestem or other native bunchgrass rather than in isolated bare soil or rich garden beds. It reseeds itself each year on undisturbed, lightly vegetated glade rock but rarely persists where soil is improved or mulched.

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown plants or rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, rocky soil at a glade edge or rock garden margin, since seed germination is slow and uneven compared with division or cuttings.

directions: Grow in rocky, well-drained soil at the sunny-to-lightly-shaded margins of glades and open woods, where this low, trailing perennial naturally sprawls over bare ground and outcrop edges across the southern and central Interior Highlands. Finely divided leaves carry dense rounded clusters of rose-pink to lavender flowers that open from spring through fall, slowing only in the hottest part of summer, when shearing the plant back encourages a fresh flush of bloom. It tolerates both full sun and the dappled afternoon shade found at the wooded edge of a glade, making it more flexible than many true glade specialists. Good drainage is essential, since the trailing stems root readily where they touch moist soil but rot in standing water.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto thin, gravelly soil so winter cold naturally stratifies it, or divide established clumps in early spring; this cold-hardy Great Plains native reaches its eastern limit on Ozark glades and prairies.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly or rocky prairie and glade soil in full sun, the dry open ground this low, mounding perennial favors from the Great Plains east into Ozark limestone and dolomite glades. Unlike night-blooming evening primroses, its bright yellow four-petaled flowers, carried above finely serrated leaves that give the plant its common name, stay open through the day and attract a steady stream of bees. It forms a tidy, woody-based mound rather than spreading aggressively, and tolerates extreme drought and poor soil once its deep root system is established. Avoid rich, moist garden beds, which cause it to sprawl and decline faster than it would on bare rock.

planting.note: Scatter seed over bare mineral soil or fine gravel in fall, pressing it in without burying, so it can germinate with autumn rains and overwinter as a small rosette ahead of spring bloom.

directions: Grow in bare, thin, well-drained soil over chert, sandstone, or limestone in full sun, the exposed glade and barrens ground across the south-central United States where this diminutive annual is easy to overlook until it blooms. Thread-like leaves give almost no visual bulk to the plant, so the small pink to nearly white four-petaled flowers that open in morning sun seem to float just above bare rock. It germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a flattened rosette, and completes its life cycle by early summer, well before the driest part of the season. Once established in suitably lean, open ground it self-sows dependably without becoming weedy.

planting.note: Direct sow where plants are to grow, since the deep taproot makes this species difficult to transplant successfully once established beyond the seedling stage.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun, the open glade, dry prairie, and barrens ground scattered across the Ozark region where this slender annual (sometimes biennial) is found. Each upright stem ends in a dense, tightly packed cylindrical spike of bright pink flowers with fringed lower petals, giving the inflorescence a distinctive look often compared to a tiny procession or candle. It develops a deep taproot quickly, which makes the plant notably drought tolerant but intolerant of transplanting once past the seedling stage. It reseeds in open, lightly disturbed ground without becoming aggressive, fitting well into a lean glade or dry meadow planting.

subcategory: native rock glade and barrens evergreen perennial

planting.note: Plant divided offsets or nursery-grown plants in spring into sharply drained rocky or sandy soil, since this species rots quickly if sited in heavy clay or poorly drained ground.

directions: Grow in sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun, the sandstone and novaculite glades and barrens of the Ouachita Mountains and adjacent Ozark and Gulf Coastal fringe where this stemless yucca is native. Its narrow, flexible, finely fiber-edged leaves form a low basal clump that is noticeably softer and less rigid than the common eastern yucca, and in late spring a tall flower stalk rises three to five feet above the foliage bearing pendant, creamy-white bell-shaped flowers pollinated at night by yucca moths. Once established it is essentially indestructible in lean, fast-draining soil, tolerating extreme heat and drought while slowly increasing by short basal offsets. It resents rich, moist garden soil and heavy mulch, both of which invite crown rot.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, open gravel or thin rocky soil after the last frost, choosing the barest, least vegetated patches available since this fine-textured annual cannot compete with taller or denser plant growth.

directions: Plant in bare, thin soil over chert, limestone, or sand in full sun, the open glade and dry prairie habitat scattered from Kansas and Missouri south through Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas where this wiry little annual grows. Narrow leaves and slender stems carry small white, star-shaped flowers along a one-sided, gently curling cyme, a structural trait typical of the borage family and the source of the genus name, which refers to flowers turning toward the sun. It completes its life cycle quickly over summer, setting seed ahead of the driest weather, and depends on bare, lightly vegetated rock or gravel free of taller competing plants. Once established in suitably open ground it self-sows reliably without becoming weedy.
